title: The Plaza de la Merced to the Mound at Vauvenargues: Picasso, the Rope, and the Grey Painting
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Málaga, the birth on the Plaza de la Merced
stops.date_confidence: attested; the civil birth record gives the hour. The baptismal date of 10 November is standard in the biographies and was not independently confirmed against the parish register in this pass.
stops.campa: On the Plaza de la Merced, in the Casas de Campos at number fifteen, a son is born to José Ruiz Blasco, drawing master at the provincial school, and María Picasso López, at about a quarter past eleven at night. The civil register takes the hour down. Two weeks later the parish of Santiago Apóstol enters him under a chain of saints' names long enough to fill a line of the book, and the family calls him Pablo. His father keeps pigeons and paints them; the plaza outside is full of the same birds.
suggested_refs: The Casa Natal on the Plaza de la Merced, Málaga, now the birthplace museum
The baptismal register of Santiago Apóstol, Málaga
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' (civil birth record: 23:15, 25 October 1881)
es.wikipedia, 'Plaza de la Merced (Málaga)' (numbers 15-20, Casas de Campos, identified as the birthplace; square at 36.723297, -4.417508)
Musée national Picasso-Paris chronology, per dossier synthesis

stops.name: A Coruña, the father's classroom on the Atlantic
stops.date_confidence: the year 1891 is attested and the boy's enrolment in 1892; the month of the family's arrival is not given in reachable sources and 1 September is a default.
stops.campa: José Ruiz takes a post at the School of Fine Arts in A Coruña and moves the household from the Andalusian coast to the Atlantic one, into rain and fog and a language nobody at home speaks. Some accounts put the appointment at the Instituto da Guarda instead; the two institutions are separate and the conflation is common. The father hates the city. The son enrolls in his father's school at ten and begins the academic drill, casts and anatomy and the figure in charcoal, and within three years the drawing has gone past the man teaching it.
suggested_refs: The Escuela de Bellas Artes de A Coruña, where father and son were master and pupil
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' ('The family moved to A Coruña in 1891, where his father became a professor at the School of Fine Arts')
Verification note: the Instituto da Guarda attribution circulating in the dossier is an error, flagged and not resolved here

stops.name: A Coruña, the death of Conchita
stops.date_confidence: January 1895 attested; the exact day is not given in reachable sources. The vow to give up painting if she were spared is family tradition, carried by the museums' biographical material and by no document.
stops.campa: María de la Concepción, called Conchita, seven years old, dies of diphtheria in the Atlantic winter. The family tells afterward that Pablo bargained with God, offering his painting for her life, and that the bargain was refused. No paper carries the vow, only the household's memory of it. What is on record is the leaving: the father applies for Barcelona, the household packs, and the city that took the girl is behind them by autumn. Biographers date his lifelong preoccupation with death to this room. He is thirteen.
suggested_refs: Museu Picasso Barcelona and Musée national Picasso-Paris biographical material on the A Coruña years
sources: Musée national Picasso-Paris / Museu Picasso Barcelona biographical materials, per dossier synthesis [R]
Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' (A Coruña residence 1891-1895)

stops.name: Barcelona, Carrer de la Mercè and the week-long examination
stops.date_confidence: the 1895 move and the entrance examination are attested; the month is not fixed in reachable sources.
stops.campa: The family settles at Carrer de la Mercè number three and José Ruiz teaches at La Llotja, where his son sits the entrance examination for the advanced classes. Candidates are allowed a month for it. The boy finishes in about a week and is admitted at thirteen. Two years later he paints Science and Charity, a doctor at a sickbed with his fingers on a dying woman's wrist while a nun holds out a cup and a child, his father posed as the doctor. It goes to the National Exhibition in Madrid and comes back with an honorable mention.
suggested_refs: Science and Charity (1897), Museu Picasso, Barcelona
The Escola de Belles Arts de la Llotja, where both Ruiz and his son were on the rolls
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' (entrance examination completed in about one week; Science and Charity and its honorable mention)

stops.name: Madrid, San Fernando and the Prado
stops.date_confidence: enrolment at sixteen in 1897 is attested; the month is a default and the withdrawal date is not fixed in reachable sources.
stops.campa: He is sixteen when he enrolls at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando in the Palacio de Goyeneche on the Calle de Alcalá, and he attends badly. The teaching is the same teaching, copied out of Paris a generation late. A short walk east, in the Prado, hang Velázquez, Goya, and El Greco, and he goes there instead and copies. He is still answering Velázquez sixty years later. In 1936 the Republic will name him the Prado's director, a post he holds from Paris.
suggested_refs: The Museo del Prado galleries of Velázquez, Goya, and El Greco
The Republican decree of September 1936 naming Picasso director of the Prado
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' ('Attended Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando at age 16')
Wikipedia, 'Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando' (40.4178, -3.7007, Calle de Alcalá 13)
Wikipedia, 'Museo del Prado' (lists Picasso as director 1936-1939)

stops.name: Horta de Sant Joan, the months with Pallarès
stops.date_confidence: the stay is attested to 1898-1899 and the return visit to 1909; the months are not specified in reachable sources.
stops.campa: He leaves Barcelona for the Terra Alta with his friend Manuel Pallarès and stays months at the family farm above Horta de Ebro, among olive terraces and mules and men who work stone. He calls the stay formative afterward and keeps calling it that. Eleven years later he comes back with Fernande Olivier and paints the same hill as a stack of tilted planes: the reservoir, the palm, the houses cut into facets and folded into the rock behind them, under a sky left nearly bare.
suggested_refs: The Pallarès farmhouse above Horta de Sant Joan
The 1909 Horta canvases, including The Reservoir and Houses on the Hill
sources: Wikipedia, 'Horta de Sant Joan' (Picasso's 1898-1899 stay with Pallarès and his 1909 return)

stops.name: Barcelona, Els Quatre Gats
stops.date_confidence: February 1900 for the exhibition is attested; the day is not given.
stops.campa: Carrer Montsió three, a modernista tavern built by Puig i Cadafalch and run on the model of the Chat Noir, is where the young painters of Barcelona argue. He draws its menu card. In February the main room is hung with his portraits of the circle, mostly charcoal, pinned close together: Casagemas, Pallarès, Sabartés, the whole table looking back at itself. It is his first one-man show. It sells almost nothing. Carles Casagemas is the closest of them, and the two settle on Paris for the autumn.
suggested_refs: The Els Quatre Gats menu card designed by Picasso, 1899-1900
The charcoal portraits of the Quatre Gats circle, Museu Picasso, Barcelona
sources: Wikipedia, 'Els Quatre Gats' (first solo exhibition, February 1900; menu and poster design)
Museu Picasso Barcelona chronology, per dossier synthesis

stops.name: Paris, the Champ de Mars and the Spanish section
stops.date_confidence: the 1900 trip is attested; autumn is the usual dating and the day is not fixed in reachable sources.
stops.campa: He comes up from Barcelona with Casagemas for the Exposition Universelle, nineteen years old and with almost no French. His canvas Last Moments, a priest at a deathbed, hangs in the Spanish section of the fair. He and Casagemas take a Montmartre studio lent by a compatriot. He meets the poet Max Jacob, who has no Spanish; for a while the two of them talk by drawing. He goes home to Spain for Christmas. Three years on he will lay another picture over Last Moments, and the deathbed will survive only as a shadow under radiography.
suggested_refs: Last Moments (1900), overpainted and now visible only by X-ray beneath La Vie
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' (first Paris trip 1900; Last Moments in the Spanish section; meeting with Max Jacob)

stops.name: Madrid, the news from the boulevard de Clichy
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested to 17 February 1901. Picasso's own whereabouts are given in the sources only as 'in Spain'; the Madrid pin is where he is generally placed for the winter of 1901 and is not documented for that day. The stop is his because the hearing was his; the café is not his stop.
stops.campa: He is in Spain when the news comes. Carles Casagemas, refused by Germaine Pichot, has gathered her and a few friends for dinner at the Café de l'Hippodrome on the boulevard de Clichy, produced a revolver, fired at her, and shot himself through the temple. He was twenty. No account puts Picasso nearer than the far side of the Pyrenees. What follows in the painting is blue: beggars, the blind, hands too long for the wrists, the palette narrowed almost to a single cold register, and Casagemas laid out with a candle burning at his head.
suggested_refs: The site of the Café de l'Hippodrome, boulevard de Clichy, Paris, where Casagemas died
The Death of Casagemas (1901) and Evocation: The Burial of Casagemas (1901)
sources: Musée national Picasso-Paris and standard biographical scholarship, synthesized across encyclopedic sources (date, circumstances, Picasso absent in Spain)
Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' (Blue Period beginning 1901; signature shortened to 'Picasso')

stops.name: Barcelona, La Vie
stops.date_confidence: 1903 attested; the month is not fixed in reachable sources. The picture's iconography is disputed and no reading is treated as settled here.
stops.campa: Back in Barcelona he paints a canvas over a canvas: beneath La Vie lies the Last Moments that hung at the world's fair. A man and a naked woman stand at the left, a robed mother with an infant at the right, two studies of huddled figures between them. Radiography shows the man began as a self-portrait and ended wearing Casagemas's face. Scholars have read it as sex set against maternity and as guilt over the dead friend's refused love, and no reading has carried the others with it. What is the man's hand pointing at? No two accounts agree.
suggested_refs: La Vie (1903), Cleveland Museum of Art
Technical studies of the underpainting of La Vie
sources: Dossier synthesis of catalogue raisonné and museum scholarship [R on the iconography]
Cleveland Museum of Art, provenance and technical record

stops.name: Paris, the Bateau-Lavoir
stops.date_confidence: the permanent move is attested to 1904; the month is a default. Jarry died in November 1907 and the transfer of the revolver is undated within the Bateau-Lavoir years.
stops.campa: He takes a room in a wooden tenement at thirteen rue Ravignan, on a hillside, where the floors do not meet the walls and one tap serves the building. Fernande Olivier moves in. Max Jacob sleeps in the bed by day while Picasso works by night; Guillaume Apollinaire comes up the hill and stays. Alfred Jarry's revolver, the one fired at Le Coudray-Montceaux, passes to him after Jarry's death, and he keeps it, collects several of the manuscripts, and draws the portrait. The blue drains out of the painting. Harlequins arrive, and the colour of terracotta.
stops.quote: The smell of opium is the least stupid smell in the world.
stops.quote_source: Picasso, as recorded by Jean Cocteau, Opium: The Diary of an Addict (1932), p. 63
suggested_refs: The Bateau-Lavoir at 13 rue Ravignan, Place Émile-Goudeau, Montmartre
Picasso's portrait drawing of Alfred Jarry and his Jarry manuscripts
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bateau-Lavoir' (address, dates, the circle)

stops.name: Gósol, the inn under the Pyrenees
stops.date_confidence: the stay is attested from spring to mid-August 1906; the arrival day is not fixed. The Stein portrait is dated 1905-1906, with the head repainted from memory in the autumn of 1906.
stops.campa: He takes Fernande Olivier over the mountains to Gósol, a village high in the Catalan range with one inn, Cal Tampanada, and they stay from spring to the middle of August. The palette turns to ochre and rose. The figures lose their particular faces and gain something closer to masks. In Paris, Gertrude Stein has sat for her portrait eighty or ninety times and he has painted the head out. He repaints it from memory that autumn without asking her to sit again. She keeps the canvas until she dies in July 1946 and leaves it to the Metropolitan Museum.
suggested_refs: Portrait of Gertrude Stein (1905-1906), Metropolitan Museum of Art, bequest of the sitter
sources: Wikipedia, 'Gósol' (dates of the stay, the inn, the change of style)
Wikipedia, 'Portrait of Gertrude Stein' (eighty or ninety sittings; head repainted from memory in autumn 1906; bequeathed at Stein's death, 27 July 1946)

segments.name: A Pair of Climbers Roped Together

stops.name: Paris, the masks in the Trocadéro
stops.date_confidence: 1907 attested; the month is not fixed. Picasso's account of the visit as a revelation is given decades afterward and is a retrospective dramatization, not a contemporaneous record.
stops.campa: The ethnographic museum in the old Trocadéro Palace is filthy, badly lit, and stacked with objects hauled home from the colonies: masks from West Africa, figures from the Congo and from Oceania. He tells the story later as an exorcism, the afternoon he understood that the objects were weapons made against a hostile world rather than sculpture to be admired, and that painting had the same job. The telling is decades late. At the time he says nothing about it and goes on with a large canvas of five women.
stops.quote: I can hardly understand the importance given to the word research in connection with modern painting. In my opinion to search means nothing in painting. To find is the thing.
stops.quote_source: Pablo Picasso, 'Picasso Speaks' (interview with Marius de Zayas), The Arts, New York, May 1923, p. 315
suggested_refs: The collections of the Musée d'Ethnographie du Trocadéro, absorbed into the Musée de l'Homme after 1928
sources: Wikipedia, 'Musée de l'Homme' (the Trocadéro museum, 1882-1928, on the site of the demolished Trocadéro Palace)
Standard art-historical scholarship on the 1907 visit, per multiple museum chronologies
Wikiquote, Picasso, for the De Zayas passage

stops.name: Paris, Les Demoiselles d'Avignon
stops.date_confidence: the painting is dated to 1907 and the month of completion is not fixed; the first public exhibition, Salon d'Antin, 16-31 July 1916, and the MoMA purchase of November 1937 are attested.
stops.campa: Hundreds of preparatory studies stand behind it. Five women face out of a shallow, splintered space hung with drapery that has the weight of rock, and two of them wear faces that came from somewhere other than the room. Georges Braque and Henri Matisse both see it in the studio and both react with hostility, which is on record from both sides. Picasso rolls the canvas up. It is not publicly exhibited until the Salon d'Antin in July 1916, nine years on, and the Museum of Modern Art buys it in November 1937 for twenty-four thousand dollars.
stops.quote: Art is a lie that makes us realize truth, at least the truth that is given us to understand.
stops.quote_source: Pablo Picasso, 'Picasso Speaks' (interview with Marius de Zayas), The Arts, New York, May 1923, p. 315
suggested_refs: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907), Museum of Modern Art, New York
The Blaue Reiter almanac (Munich, 1912), in which Kandinsky and Franz Marc set Picasso's work beside Bavarian glass painting, Russian folk prints, and African and Pacific masks
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso'
Wikipedia, 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' (Salon d'Antin, 16-31 July 1916; MoMA acquisition November 1937, $24,000; hostile first reactions of Braque and Matisse)

stops.name: Céret, painting beside Braque
stops.date_confidence: the summer of 1911 at Céret with Braque is attested, and a further stay in 1913; the arrival day is not fixed.
stops.campa: He takes rooms in a Catalan town on the French side of the border, in a country of cherry orchards, and Braque follows. From 1908 the two of them work at one problem with such closeness that the canvases of these months can be told apart only with difficulty and sometimes not at all, and many are left unsigned. Ropes, stencilled letters, the corner of a newspaper, a tuning peg. Dealers and painters come down after them until the town has a name in the trade. Braque is asked about it in 1954.
stops.quote: It was rather like a pair of climbers roped together.
stops.quote_source: Georges Braque, interview with Dora Vallier, 1954
suggested_refs: The Céret canvases of summer 1911
Musée d'Art Moderne de Céret
sources: Wikipedia, 'Céret'
Wikipedia, 'Georges Braque' (the 1908-1912 exchange; Céret, summer 1911; works at times indistinguishable)
Wikiquote, Braque, sourced entry for the Vallier interview

stops.name: Paris, the oilcloth and the rope
stops.date_confidence: 1912 attested; the month is the usual dating and the day is not fixed. Priority between Picasso's pasted oilcloth and Braque's papier collé is disputed and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Onto a small oval canvas he glues a piece of printed oilcloth bought for the purpose, machine-made and pretending to be woven cane, and around the whole he ties a length of rope for a frame. The letters JOU, from a newspaper masthead, sit at the left. Nothing in the picture is described. Things are brought in and set down. Braque is cutting and pasting paper the same season and the two developments run together, so that the question of who did it first opens at once and stays open.
stops.quote: Cubism is no different from any other school of painting.
stops.quote_source: Pablo Picasso, 'Picasso Speaks' (interview with Marius de Zayas), The Arts, New York, May 1923, p. 319
suggested_refs: Still Life with Chair Caning (1912), Musée national Picasso-Paris
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' (Still Life with Chair Caning, pasted oilcloth, rope frame, routinely called the first modern collage)
Wikipedia, 'Georges Braque' (concurrent papier collé)

stops.name: Avignon, the mobilization
stops.date_confidence: attested that Picasso was living at Avignon at the outbreak of the war and that Braque and Derain were mobilized; 2 August is the French mobilization date and not a documented date for the parting itself.
stops.campa: He is working in the Midi when general mobilization is posted. Braque and André Derain go to the station and he sees them off; he is a Spanish national and Spain is neutral, and he does not go. Braque will be trepanned after a head wound and come back to a different studio. The four years of two men working as one hand end on a railway platform in August. He had spent the summer of 1912 at Sorgues, an hour up the Rhône, using a rented house as a laboratory for the pasted pictures; that country is finished now too. He goes back to Paris alone.
suggested_refs: The Sorgues summer house of 1912, working ground for Synthetic Cubism
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' ('Living there at outbreak of World War I')
Wikipedia, 'Georges Braque' (Braque and Derain enlist in 1914, ending the collaborative phase; Picasso, a Spanish national, does not serve)
The Sorgues stay is standard in Picasso chronologies and was not independently confirmed in this pass [R]

stops.name: Paris, the death of Eva Gouel
stops.date_confidence: the death date is attested across the standard chronologies; the cause is usually given as tuberculosis complicated by other disease, and the clinic is outside the city and not named in reachable sources. The Paris pin is the city, not an address.
stops.campa: Marcelle Humbert, whom he calls Eva and whose name he has written into the paintings, J'aime Eva, Ma Jolie, has been ill a long time. The sources agree on tuberculosis with something else complicating it and agree on little more; the clinic where she dies stands outside the city and none of them names it. He had left Fernande Olivier for her in 1911. He is thirty-four. The war is in its second winter and half the people he used to drink with are at the front.
suggested_refs: Ma Jolie (1911-1912) and the canvases inscribed J'aime Eva
sources: Dossier synthesis, corroborated across standard Picasso biographical chronologies (death 14 December 1915)
Catalogue titles and painted inscriptions corroborating the relationship [R on the biographical narrative]

stops.name: Rome, joining Diaghilev's company
stops.date_confidence: February 1917 for the Rome gathering is attested. The onward stops at Naples and Pompeii are standard in the biographies and were not independently confirmed in this pass [R].
stops.campa: Jean Cocteau talks him into the theatre, and Sergei Diaghilev shuts the collaborators up together in Rome through the winter to force Parade into being: Cocteau's scenario, Erik Satie's score, Léonide Massine's choreography, Picasso on curtain, sets, and costumes. Igor Stravinsky, travelling with the same company, sits for a portrait drawing, and a story about the drawing being seized at a frontier as fortification plans circulates in several versions. He goes on with them to Naples and to the ruins of Pompeii. In a rehearsal room he watches the dancers and picks out a Ukrainian of the second rank, Olga Khokhlova.
suggested_refs: Picasso's 1917 portrait drawing of Stravinsky
The Pompeii excavations, linked by later scholarship to the statuesque figures of the postwar years
sources: Wikipedia, 'Parade (ballet)' ('In February 1917, all the collaborators met in Rome to begin working on Parade')

stops.name: Paris, the Théâtre du Châtelet: Parade
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: The curtain rises on a painted Harlequin, a winged horse, a girl acrobat, and behind it a fairground sideshow whose two managers are built into cubist constructions of cardboard and cloth ten feet high, able to do very little but stamp. Satie's score takes in a typewriter and a siren. The house objects loudly and objects hardest to the costumes, and it comes close to a riot before the applause carries the evening. Apollinaire's programme note, written for the evening, puts a word into French that has no movement attached to it yet.
stops.quote: une sorte de surréalisme (a kind of surrealism)
stops.quote_source: Guillaume Apollinaire, programme note for the premiere of Parade, Théâtre du Châtelet, 18 May 1917
suggested_refs: Picasso's Parade drop curtain, Centre Pompidou

stops.name: Paris, rue Daru: the marriage to Olga
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; postponed from May 1918 owing to Khokhlova's foot injury and surgery. Apollinaire is named as a witness in much of the literature and not by the record, which gives Cocteau and Jacob only.
stops.campa: They are married in the Russian Orthodox cathedral on the rue Daru, in the rite with the crowns held over the heads of the couple, the ceremony pushed back from May because she had injured a foot and needed surgery. Cocteau and Max Jacob stand as witnesses; the literature adds Apollinaire, the record does not. He is thirty-six and marrying into a Russia that no longer exists, a colonel's daughter cut off from her family by the revolution. The contract puts them in community of property under the French code.
suggested_refs: The Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, 12 rue Daru, Paris
sources: Wikipedia, 'Olga Khokhlova' (12 July 1918, Russian Orthodox Cathedral, rue Daru; witnesses Jean Cocteau and Max Jacob; postponement from May)

stops.name: London, the Alhambra: Le Tricorne
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: He crosses to London for the Ballets Russes season and designs the drop curtain and the costumes for El sombrero de tres picos: Manuel de Falla's score, Massine's choreography, an Andalusia painted by an Andalusian for an English house. The curtain, a bullring seen past a parapet of spectators watching from the shade, goes up at the Alhambra in Leicester Square on the twenty-second of July. It is his second full production for Diaghilev. He goes on designing for the company until 1924.
suggested_refs: The Tricorne drop curtain, later hung in the Four Seasons restaurant, New York, and now at the New-York Historical Society
sources: Wikipedia, 'El sombrero de tres picos' (premiere 22 July 1919, Alhambra Theatre, London; sets and costumes by Picasso, choreography Massine, music Falla)

stops.name: Paris, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées: Le Train Bleu
stops.date_confidence: 1924 is attested for Le Train Bleu and for Mercure; the June premiere day is not independently fixed in this pass.
stops.campa: The ballets keep coming: Pulcinella in 1920 at the Opéra to Stravinsky's score, Cuadro flamenco in 1921, Mercure with Satie and Massine in 1924. For Le Train Bleu that June, Diaghilev has a small gouache of two women running on a beach enlarged to the size of a stage curtain, and Gabrielle Chanel dresses the dancers in knitted bathing costumes and quietly pays for part of the production. George Balanchine reaches the company in the same period. The curtain is the only thing of Picasso's in the piece.
suggested_refs: The Train Bleu curtain, enlarged from Picasso's gouache Two Women Running on the Beach (1922)

segments.name: Rue La Boétie and the Two Households

stops.name: Paris, 23 rue La Boétie
stops.date_confidence: the residency runs 1918-1936; the month of the move is not fixed in reachable sources. Paulo's birth on 4 February 1921 is attested. The Fontainebleau summer is attested to 1921 without exact dates.
stops.campa: Olga moves them out of Montparnasse into an eighth-arrondissement apartment with the floor above taken over as a studio, and into the life that goes with it: cook, chauffeur, dinner jackets, the Faubourg at dinner. Paulo is born in February 1921 and painted over and over, as harlequin, as pierrot, asleep. That summer they rent at Fontainebleau and he works out of the garage, producing the two large Three Musicians. Down the same street at number thirty-four a young man named Christian Dior keeps a gallery that hangs Picasso beside Dalí, Braque, and Max Jacob.
suggested_refs: Three Musicians (1921), in the two versions at MoMA and the Philadelphia Museum of Art
The Galerie Jacques Bonjean, 34 rue La Boétie

stops.name: Paris, outside the Galeries Lafayette
stops.date_confidence: January 1927 rests on Marie-Thérèse Walter's own account, given long afterward and the only source for the encounter; the day is a default within that month and the coordinate is the store she names.
stops.campa: He is forty-five and he stops a girl on the pavement outside the department store on the boulevard Haussmann. By her account, given many years later, he takes her arm and says she has an interesting face, that he would like to make her portrait, and that he is Picasso, a name that means nothing at all to her. She is seventeen. For years she is kept out of sight of the rue La Boétie, and she enters the work as a shape long before she enters it as a face: a curve, a profile cut into plaster, the letters of her name hidden among the guitars.
suggested_refs: The Marie-Thérèse canvases and plaster heads of 1927-1937
sources: Marie-Thérèse Walter's own later account as recorded in standard Picasso biographical scholarship [R as to the day and the wording]

stops.name: Boisgeloup, the plaster heads in the barn
stops.date_confidence: the purchase is attested to June 1930. The Zervos conversation is placed at Boisgeloup in the winter of 1934 and published in 1935.
stops.campa: He buys a small Normandy château near Gisors with stone outbuildings and puts a sculpture studio in them, the first room he has ever had large enough to work big. Plaster goes up in it: heads of Marie-Thérèse Walter with the nose swelled into a ridge and the eyes turned into spheres. The Vollard Suite is etched here. Christian Zervos comes out in the winter of 1934 and takes down a conversation for Cahiers d'Art. Olga's horses are in the stable and the plaster heads are in the barn, on one property, for five years.
stops.quote: There is no abstract art. You always start with something.
stops.quote_source: Pablo Picasso to Christian Zervos, 'Conversation avec Picasso,' Cahiers d'Art, X, 7-10 (1935), pp. 173-178 (Boisgeloup, winter 1934). Chipp's fuller translation continues: 'One must always begin with something. Afterwards one can remove all semblance of reality; there is no longer any danger as the idea of the object has left an indelible imprint.'
suggested_refs: The Boisgeloup plaster heads, Musée national Picasso-Paris
The Vollard Suite etchings
sources: Wikipedia, 'Château de Boisgeloup' (bought with Olga Khokhlova, June 1930; sculpture; Vollard Suite; 49°15'19"N 1°46'49"E)
Wikiquote, Picasso, sourced Zervos entry
Herschel B. Chipp, Theories of Modern Art (1968), p. 270
Note: the Julio González welded-iron collaboration belongs to González's Paris workshop, not to Boisgeloup

stops.name: Paris, the household comes apart
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1935 without a month; the sequence, discovery then birth, is fixed by Maya's birth on 5 September 1935 at Boulogne-Billancourt. Olga filed for divorce and none was ever granted.
stops.campa: A friend tells Olga about the girl and that the girl is pregnant. She takes Paulo and goes, and files for divorce; French community of property makes a real dissolution ruinous and it never happens, so she stays his wife until she dies at Cannes in February 1955. On the fifth of September, at Boulogne-Billancourt, María de la Concepción is born and called Maya, carrying the name of the sister who died in A Coruña. He registers her father unknown, since a married man may not acknowledge a child born outside the marriage. That year he paints almost nothing and writes poems instead.
suggested_refs: Picasso's surrealist poems of 1935-1936, published by Cahiers d'Art
sources: Wikipedia, 'Olga Khokhlova' (learned of the affair and the pregnancy in 1935 from a friend, filed for divorce, stayed legally married until her death 11 February 1955 in Cannes)
Wikipedia, 'Maya Widmaier-Picasso' (born 5 September 1935, Boulogne-Billancourt; registered with father unknown)

segments.name: The Grey Painting and the Occupation

stops.name: Paris, 7 rue des Grands-Augustins: thirty-five days
stops.date_confidence: attested: bombing 26 April 1937, work begun after the newspaper reports, canvas completed 4 June 1937 after 35 days. Dora Maar's dated photographs document the sequence.
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of April the Condor Legion and Italian aircraft bomb a Basque market town for something over two hours, on market day, and burn it. He reads the Paris newspapers, George Steer's account among them, hears Juan Larrea back from the north, and drops the subject he had begun for the Republic's pavilion. The canvas is three and a half metres by nearly eight and the studio he has taken with Dora Maar's help will not hold it upright, so it stands tilted. Maar photographs it at every stage in black and white, and the painting goes grey.
stops.quote: The Spanish struggle is the fight of reaction against the people, against freedom. My whole life as an artist has been nothing more than a continuous struggle against reaction and the death of art. How could anybody think for a moment that I could be in agreement with reaction and death?... In the panel on which I am working, which I shall call Guernica, and in all my recent works of art, I clearly express my abhorrence of the military caste which has sunk Spain in an ocean of pain and death.
stops.quote_source: Pablo Picasso, public statement, May 1937, published in the American Artists' Congress catalogue and reprinted in Alfred H. Barr Jr., Picasso: Forty Years of His Art (MoMA, 1939)
suggested_refs: Dora Maar's sequence of studio photographs of Guernica in progress, Musée national Picasso-Paris
The studio at 7 rue des Grands-Augustins, Paris
sources: Wikipedia, 'Guernica (painting)' (bombing date, Condor Legion, market day, studio address, 35 days, completed 4 June 1937, Steer and Larrea, Maar's photographs)
Note: Picasso was never at Gernika, and the town is not a stop on his own file

stops.name: Paris, the Spanish Pavilion
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1937 for the pavilion showing; the opening day is not fixed in this pass and the pavilion coordinate is approximate, taken from the 1937 Exposition site near the Champ de Mars.
stops.campa: It hangs in a pavilion of steel and glass put up by a government that is losing the war it is advertising, beside a cast of his own Woman with a Vase. Some of the Republic's own officials would have preferred a poster. Then the canvas travels: Scandinavia, London on the day of the Munich agreement, America from May 1939, and the Museum of Modern Art for four decades, on his stipulation that it is not to go to Spain while Spain is not a republic. It reaches Madrid in September 1981, behind bulletproof glass, and moves to the Reina Sofía in 1992.
stops.quote: Picasso's great fresco is a monument to destruction, a cry of outrage and horror amplified by the spirit of genius.
stops.quote_source: Herbert Read, 'Guernica', in A Coat of Many Colours (Routledge, 1945)
suggested_refs: The Spanish Pavilion of the 1937 Paris International Exposition
The full-size Guernica tapestry woven by Jacqueline de la Baume Durrbach for Nelson Rockefeller, hung at the United Nations from 1985 and curtained on 5 February 2003
sources: Wikipedia, 'Guernica (painting)' (pavilion, Scandinavian and London tour, arrival in London 30 September 1938, US from May 1939, MoMA loan, 1981 return to Madrid, 1992 move to the Reina Sofía)
Wikipedia, 'Château de Vauvenargues' (Woman with a Vase, second casting, shown at the Spanish Pavilion in 1937)
Wikiquote, Herbert Read

stops.name: Bern, the hour with Klee
stops.date_confidence: attested to late 1937; the day is not given in reachable sources.
stops.campa: He climbs to an apartment on the Kistlerweg to see Paul Klee, who is ill with the disease that will kill him, the skin hardening and the chest stiffening, and who is turning out in these last years the largest and blackest work of his life. They have an hour together. Munich has just hung Klee in the Degenerate Art exhibition and Germany has taken his professorship; Guernica is on tour. Braque climbs the same stairs the following year. What the two of them said to each other has not survived.
suggested_refs: Klee's apartment at Kistlerweg 6, Bern
Klee's late large-format works, Zentrum Paul Klee
sources: paul_klee.journey.json (Picasso's visit, late 1937, an hour with Klee ill; Braque the following year)

stops.name: Paris, the Galerie Renou et Colle
stops.date_confidence: the Mexique exhibition ran in the 1938-1939 season and March 1939 is the usual dating; the day is not fixed. The exhibition is corroborated in three separate journey files.
stops.campa: Marcel Duchamp has assembled a Mexican show and Frida Kahlo has crossed with seventeen paintings, ill on the voyage and unimpressed by the surrealists who invited her. Picasso comes to look, and Kandinsky comes, whose Blaue Reiter almanac had set Picasso beside Bavarian glass painting and Egyptian shadow puppets twenty-seven years earlier. Picasso gives Kahlo a pair of tortoiseshell earrings shaped like hands and teaches her a Spanish song. Her husband Diego Rivera had kept a studio off the Gare Montparnasse in the 1910s, painting cubism in Picasso's shadow.
suggested_refs: The tortoiseshell hand earrings Picasso gave Kahlo, worn in her later self-portraits
Der Blaue Reiter almanac (Piper, Munich, 1912)
sources: diego_rivera.journey.json
frida_kahlo.journey.json
wassily_kandinsky.journey.json (all three corroborate the 1939 Mexique exhibition, the earrings, and the song)

stops.name: Paris, the occupied studio and the party card
stops.date_confidence: the party membership is attested to October 1944, weeks after the Liberation, and held until his death. The Royan interval of 1939-1940 is standard in the biographies and undated by a fetched source [R]. The German officer anecdote is undated, unwitnessed, and labelled likely apocryphal.
stops.campa: He spends the first year of the war between Paris and Royan on the Atlantic, then comes back to the occupied city instead of leaving the country, though every door out stands open to him. He is barred from exhibiting and goes on painting on the rue des Grands-Augustins: flayed sheep's heads, a tomato plant on the sill, a bull's head made from a bicycle saddle and a set of handlebars. The story of the German officer shown a photograph of Guernica and told, No, you did, has no witness and no date. In October he joins the French Communist Party and stays in it until he dies.
stops.quote: this bull is a bull and this horse is a horse... If you give a meaning to certain things in my paintings it may be very true, but it is not my idea to give this meaning. What ideas and conclusions you have got I obtained too, but instinctively, unconsciously. I make the painting for the painting. I paint the objects for what they are.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Picasso on the symbolism of Guernica, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Guernica (painting)', citing the now-dead PBS supplement to 'Guernica: Testimony to War' [R: no interview, date, or translator is recoverable]
suggested_refs: Bull's Head (1942), bicycle saddle and handlebars, Musée national Picasso-Paris
sources: Dossier synthesis of standard biographical scholarship, party archives, and Picasso's contemporaneous public statement (October 1944)
Wikipedia, 'Guernica (painting)' (the officer anecdote as 'likely apocryphal')
Wikipedia, 'Royan' (confirms Picasso among historical residents, without dates)

stops.name: Paris, rue des Beaux-Arts: the auction for Artaud
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: Antonin Artaud has come out of nine years in asylums, most of it at Rodez, weighing very little and with most of his teeth gone. His friends organize a sale to keep him alive: Pierre Loeb's gallery on the rue des Beaux-Arts takes work donated by Picasso, Braque, Giacometti, Dubuffet and others, and the auction on the thirteenth of June raises what he lives on. Picasso gives without commentary, as he gives to the Spanish refugee committees. The money buys Artaud two more years.
suggested_refs: The Galerie Pierre (Pierre Loeb), rue des Beaux-Arts, Paris
sources: artaud.journey.json (the 13 June 1946 auction; donors including Picasso, Braque, Giacometti and Dubuffet)

stops.name: Antibes, the Château Grimaldi
stops.date_confidence: the six-month residency is attested to 1946; the starting month is not fixed in reachable sources.
stops.campa: The curator of the old Grimaldi castle offers him rooms on the upper floor with the sea on three sides, and he works there six months on fibrocement and plywood because canvas cannot be had: fauns with pipes, a centaur, a goat, and La Joie de vivre, a girl dancing on a shore between goats and a flute. He leaves twenty-three paintings and forty-four drawings in the building when he goes, and in December 1966 the castle takes his name. Françoise Gilot is with him, and Claude is born the following year.
stops.quote: He did not know me well at all. I am very secretive. I smile and I'm polite, but that doesn't mean that I am in agreement, or that I will do as I said I would do. It's just a screen. He thought I would react like all his other women. That was a completely wrong opinion.
stops.quote_source: Françoise Gilot, quoted via the Françoise Gilot Collection, Ursinus College [R: widely attributed to Life with Picasso (1964), an attribution not supported by any source reached]
suggested_refs: La Joie de vivre (1946) and the Antibes panels, Musée Picasso, Antibes
sources: Wikipedia, 'Musée Picasso (Antibes)' (six months' residence in 1946; 23 paintings and 44 drawings donated; renamed December 1966; 43°34'51"N 7°7'42"E)
en.wikipedia, 'Françoise Gilot' (the quoted passage, referenced to the Ursinus collection)

stops.name: Vallauris, the Madoura kilns
stops.date_confidence: the collaboration is attested from 1947 and the residence from 1948 to 1955; the starting month is not fixed.
stops.campa: A pottery town behind Golfe-Juan, its kilns half idle since the war took the market for cooking vessels. He walks into the Madoura workshop of Georges and Suzanne Ramié and starts working in clay and does not stop: thousands of pieces, some unique, some in editions the Ramiés are licensed to produce. Plates that are faces. Jugs that are women. Owls, bulls, a figure thrown on the wheel and then squeezed at the waist while still wet. The trade of the town comes back on his account, and in 1948 he moves there.
suggested_refs: The Madoura workshop of Georges and Suzanne Ramié, Vallauris
The Picasso ceramic editions, catalogued by Alain Ramié
sources: Wikipedia, 'Vallauris' ('In 1948 Picasso came to live in Vallauris, where he stayed until 1955'; the pottery revival; 43°34'50"N 7°03'14"E)
Madoura and Musée national Picasso-Paris archival material, per dossier synthesis

stops.name: Wrocław, the congress in the flattened city
stops.date_confidence: attested: the congress ran 25-28 August 1948 at the Wrocław University of Technology, and Picasso appears in the delegate list and in a photograph. The reported visit to Auschwitz on the same trip could not be confirmed by any source reached and stays unverified.
stops.campa: He travels to a Polish city three years out of the siege that flattened it, for the World Congress of Intellectuals in Defence of Peace at the technical university: some six hundred delegates from forty-six countries, Brecht, Neruda, Éluard, Aragon, the Joliot-Curies, Julian Huxley. He is photographed among them. The congress is organized from Moscow, and it is the start of the peace movement he belongs to for the rest of his life. Several accounts have him going on to Auschwitz during the same trip. Nothing reachable confirms it.
suggested_refs: The delegate photographs of the Wrocław congress, 25-28 August 1948
sources: Wikipedia, 'World Congress of Intellectuals in Defense of Peace' (dates, venue, ~600 delegates from 46 countries, Picasso in the delegate list and photograph)
The Auschwitz visit is asserted in the background dossier and was not independently verified [R]

stops.name: Paris, the Salle Pleyel: the dove
stops.date_confidence: the lithograph is dated 9 January 1949, the Paris congress to April 1949, and Paloma's birth to 19 April 1949 at Vallauris. The three were conflated into a single date in the working dossier and are separated here.
stops.campa: On the ninth of January he pulls a lithograph of a pigeon, white on black, the bird his father used to paint. Louis Aragon takes it for the poster of the peace congress meeting at the Salle Pleyel in April, and the pigeon becomes a dove, and the dove becomes the emblem of half the world's demonstrations for the next forty years. On the nineteenth of April, at Vallauris, Françoise Gilot gives birth to a daughter, and they name her Paloma, which is the Spanish for the bird on the poster. He is sixty-seven.
suggested_refs: Dove (La Colombe), lithograph, 9 January 1949
The poster of the 1949 World Congress of Partisans for Peace, Salle Pleyel, Paris
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' ('On 9 January 1949, Picasso created Dove, a black and white lithograph'; used for the 1949 World Peace Council poster)
Wikipedia, 'World Peace Council' (La Colombe chosen as the congress emblem)
Wikipedia, 'Paloma Picasso' (born 19 April 1949, Vallauris; named for the peace symbol)
Wikipedia, 'Salle Pleyel' (48.8769944, 2.3010361)

stops.name: Vallauris, the Temple of Peace
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1952; the months of work are not fixed in reachable sources.
stops.campa: A deconsecrated Romanesque chapel in the castle courtyard, barrel-vaulted and small. He covers the two long walls on plywood panels curved to fit the vault: on one side war, a black chariot, a figure carrying a bloodied sword and a basket of skulls, hands full of weapons; on the other peace, a child ploughing with a winged horse, dancers, a woman with a bowl. The two walls face each other across a space narrow enough to stand in the middle of and touch neither. He calls the room a Temple of Peace and hands it over to the state.
suggested_refs: La Guerre et la Paix (1952), Musée national Picasso, Vallauris
sources: Wikipedia, 'Vallauris' (the War and Peace mural described as one of the major artworks of the period)

stops.name: Cannes, the Villa La Californie
stops.date_confidence: the purchase is attested to 1955 and the occupancy to 1961; the month of the move is not fixed in reachable sources.
stops.campa: He buys a Belle Époque villa above Cannes at 22 avenue Coste Belle, art nouveau ironwork, palms in the garden, tall arched windows, and moves in with Jacqueline Roque, whom he met three years earlier at the Madoura pottery. Olga has died at Cannes in February. He paints the rooms themselves now, over and over: the studio with its stove and its easel and its heaped clutter, the windows, the palms outside them, Jacqueline sitting in a rocking chair with her knees drawn up.
suggested_refs: The Ateliers series of La Californie, 1955-1957
sources: Wikipedia, 'Villa La Californie' (22 Avenue Coste Belle; bought 1955; moved in with Jacqueline Roque; left for Mougins in 1961 when development blocked the sea view; 43°33'2.79"N 7°2'31.57"E)
Wikipedia, 'Vallauris' (Jacqueline Roque worked at Madoura, met Picasso there in 1952)

stops.name: Cannes, Lump and the forty-four Meninas
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for Lump's arrival, and to 17 August - 30 December 1957 for the Meninas series.
stops.campa: David Douglas Duncan brings up a dachshund he had bought as company for his Afghan hound Kubla, who would not have him. Picasso feeds the dog off his own plate at lunch, paints the dog on the plate, and the dog stays six years, running the house over the boxer Yan and the goat Esmeralda. Between the seventeenth of August and the thirtieth of December that year he makes forty-four canvases after Velázquez's Las Meninas, the pictures he had first stood in front of at seventeen. Velázquez's Spanish mastiff is gone from them. In fifteen there is a dachshund.
stops.quote: This was a love affair. Picasso would take Lump in his arms. He would feed him from his hand. Hell, that little dog just took over. He ran the damn house.
stops.quote_source: David Douglas Duncan, quoted in 'How Picasso fell for a dachshund,' The Independent, 1 May 2006
suggested_refs: The 44 Las Meninas variations, Museu Picasso, Barcelona
David Douglas Duncan, Picasso & Lump: A Dachshund's Odyssey (Thames & Hudson, 2006)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Lump (dog)' (19 April 1957 arrival at La Californie; the painted plate; six years; Yan and Esmeralda; 44 studies, 15 with Lump; Duncan's Afghan hound named Kubla)
Note: Duncan's Kubla and Picasso's own Afghan hound Kabul are two different dogs and are not to be merged

stops.name: Vauvenargues, Cézanne's mountain bought
stops.date_confidence: the purchase is attested to September 1958 and the residence to 1959-1961; the day is not given. The Wikipedia article on the château and the geography lens disagree slightly on the coordinate (43.5539, 5.6039 against 43.5542, 5.6044); the infobox value is used and the discrepancy is not resolved.
stops.campa: He buys a seventeenth-century château on the north flank of Mont Sainte-Victoire and tells his dealer over the telephone that he has bought Cézanne's Sainte-Victoire. Not a painting of it. The mountain Cézanne worked over for thirty years stands at the end of the terrace. The house is cold and enormous, a stone staircase, rooms he paints in and rooms he never enters, and he lives there with Jacqueline into 1961 before deciding it is too severe to keep as a home. He never sells it.
suggested_refs: The Château de Vauvenargues below Mont Sainte-Victoire, still private property
sources: Wikipedia, 'Château de Vauvenargues' (purchase September 1958; 'J'ai acheté la Sainte-Victoire'; residence and later burial)

stops.name: Vallauris, the town hall, in secret
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: He is seventy-nine and she is thirty-four, and they marry at the town hall of the pottery town in complete secrecy, six years after he stopped living there. Olga's death in 1955 has made it legally possible at last. Nobody is told: not the children, not the dealers, not the press, which learns of it afterward. Jacqueline is at his side for the twelve years remaining and controls who gets through the door. They had met nine years earlier at the Madoura pottery, where she worked.
suggested_refs: The Vallauris town hall, Place Jacques Cavasse
sources: Wikipedia, 'Vallauris' (married Jacqueline Roque 'amid the greatest secrecy at Vallauris town hall in 1961')
Dossier synthesis, Musée national Picasso-Paris (2 March 1961)

stops.name: Mougins, the Mas Notre-Dame-de-Vie
stops.date_confidence: the move is attested to 1961 and the residence runs to 1973; the month is not fixed. The Chicago sculpture was designed in 1962-1963, which places Kabul in the household by then.
stops.campa: They move to a farmhouse on a hillside above Mougins, beside a twelfth-century chapel, with the sea in the distance and a gate that stays shut. He is eighty. An Afghan hound called Kabul lives there among the doves and the goats, and when Chicago asks for a sculpture for its civic plaza he says the head is Kabul's. The last twelve years are the most productive of his life by sheer count: musketeers, matadors, painters and models, hundreds of canvases a year, worked fast and dated like a diary on the back.
suggested_refs: The Chicago Picasso, Daley Plaza, designed 1962-1963
The late Mougins canvases, musketeers and painter-and-model subjects
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mougins' (the farmhouse beside the chapel, 1961-1973)
Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' (Picasso said the Chicago figure represented the head of an Afghan hound named Kabul)

stops.name: Mougins, the last morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; heart failure following pulmonary edema.
stops.campa: He dies on the morning of the eighth of April at Notre-Dame-de-Vie, ninety-one years old, of heart failure after pulmonary edema, with Jacqueline there. He had been working the night before. Lump the dachshund died on the twenty-ninth of March, ten days earlier, aged sixteen or seventeen; the dossier places the death in Germany and the source does not support it. There is no will. In May, at the Palais des Papes in Avignon, two hundred and one paintings he helped choose that spring open to a public that mostly reads them as an old man in a hurry.
suggested_refs: The Avignon Arts Festival exhibition at the Palais des Papes, opened May 1973
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pablo Picasso' (died 8 April 1973, Mougins; assisted in assembling 201 paintings for the Avignon festival, opened at the Palais des Papes in May 1973)
Wikipedia, 'Lump (dog)' (died 29 March 1973, aged 16-17, ten days before Picasso; no place of death given)
Musée national Picasso-Paris chronology and contemporary press, per dossier synthesis

stops.name: Vauvenargues, the earthen mound
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The working dossier gave 10 April, which is wrong.
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of April he is buried on the shaded terrace before the main entrance of the château, in a sleeping position beneath an earthen mound, and the bronze Woman with a Vase is set over him, the second cast of the figure that stood in the Spanish Pavilion in 1937. Jacqueline keeps the funeral small and keeps much of the family away from it. Six years of litigation follow, and end with the French state accepting payment of the inheritance tax in art. Jacqueline is laid beside him in 1986.
suggested_refs: The grave at the Château de Vauvenargues, marked by Woman with a Vase (1933, second casting)
The Musée national Picasso-Paris at the Hôtel Salé, formed from the 1979 dation and reopened 25 October 2014, on what would have been his birthday
sources: Wikipedia, 'Château de Vauvenargues' (buried 16 April 1973 in a sleeping position beneath an earthen mound; Woman with a Vase placed on the grave; Jacqueline buried beside him)
